text: Every circuit, gradient, and training loop in this course runs through one of two real, actively maintained open-source libraries. Knowing what each one is actually for will save you from fighting the wrong tool later.

PennyLane, built by Xanadu, treats a quantum circuit as a differentiable function called a QNode, bound to a device, and plugs directly into PyTorch, TensorFlow, and JAX. Qiskit Machine Learning, IBM's library, leans toward ready-made building blocks: EstimatorQNN and SamplerQNN wrappers, a prebuilt VQC classifier, and a FidelityQuantumKernel you can hand straight to scikit-learn. Underneath, both rely on identical math, state preparation, ansatz, measurement, and parameter-shift gradients — only the API surface differs.

The two libraries converge on the same concepts with different names. What PennyLane calls a device, Qiskit calls a backend, estimator, or sampler. Both call the trainable circuit structure an ansatz. PennyLane's encoding template is Qiskit's feature map. And PennyLane's QNode corresponds to Qiskit's EstimatorQNN or SamplerQNN. Learning either library's documentation makes the other's far easier to read.

Every lab in this course runs on a classical simulator, PennyLane's default-qubit device or Qiskit's AerSimulator, not real quantum hardware. This is a deliberate, honest choice: simulation gives you an exact, noise-free environment to learn how variational training actually behaves. What it does not prove is that a technique will work the same way on real NISQ hardware, where gate errors, readout errors, and decoherence can meaningfully worsen training.
Next lesson closes out the foundations chapter with the single most important disclaimer in the whole course: the precise claim about quantum advantage that this course does, and does not, make.
